legacy.text: The Moapa did not last as a separate forest. It was transferred whole to the Toiyabe National Forest in 1915.

today.name: Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest
today.note: By way of the Toiyabe, which took in the whole Moapa in 1915.

related.note: Enlarged the Moapa National Forest that Executive Order 908 had created out of the Charleston and Vegas forests.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2162 transferred the entire Moapa National Forest to the Toiyabe.

legacy.text: The first Marquette National Forest lasted six years. Its land passed to the Michigan National Forest in 1915 and the Marquette name was dropped; that land later became part of the Hiawatha National Forest.

today.name: Marquette National Forest
today.note: Merged into the Michigan National Forest in 1915. A second, different Marquette (the renamed Michigan) was abolished in 1962.

today.name: Hiawatha National Forest
today.note: Took in the lands of the second Marquette National Forest in 1962.

related.note: The Michigan National Forest, created the next day, took in the Marquette's land in 1915.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2163 passed the Marquette's land to the Michigan National Forest and discontinued the Marquette name.

legacy.text: The Nevada National Forest absorbed the whole Toiyabe in 1932 and was itself abolished in 1957, divided between the Humboldt and a revived Toiyabe.

today.name: Nevada National Forest
today.note: Abolished effective October 1, 1957, and divided between the Humboldt and the Toiyabe.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 5863 folded the entire Toiyabe National Forest into the Nevada.

Public Land Order 1487, signed by Assistant Secretary of the Interior Roger Ernst, abolished the Nevada National Forest effective October 1, 1957 and divided it between the Humboldt and a revived Toiyabe.

reception.text: The Pinconning Press and the Clare Sentinel ran the same short, factual item: the state land commissioner had been told that 134,630 acres in Ogemaw, Oscoda and Alcona counties near the Au Sable had been set aside as a national forest reserve.
reception.source: Pinconning Press and Clare Sentinel, Mar. 11–12, 1909 (Digital Michigan Newspapers)

political_impact.text: Michigan's land commissioner, Huntley S. Russell, was notified from Washington of the new forest in northern Michigan.
political_impact.source: Pinconning Press and Clare Sentinel, Mar. 11–12, 1909

legacy.text: The Michigan took in the first Marquette's land in 1915, was renamed the Marquette in 1931, and was abolished in 1962, when its lands went to the Hiawatha National Forest.

related.note: The Michigan absorbed the first Marquette National Forest in 1915.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2163 added the Marquette National Forest's land to the Michigan.
Proclamation 1938 renamed the Michigan National Forest the Marquette National Forest.
Executive Order 10993 transferred the lands of the Marquette National Forest, as proclaimed in 1931, to the Hiawatha National Forest.

uncertain: The 134,630 acres reported in the Michigan press differs slightly from the Forest Service's official 132,770 acres; the reason is not known.

legacy.text: The Superior grew into one of the best-known forests in the system, home to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

today.name: Superior National Forest
today.note: Home to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

uncertain: Whether Minnesota newspapers noticed the Superior's creation in 1909 is not known; no Minnesota collection could be searched by phrase and date.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 5863 folded the whole Toiyabe into the Nevada National Forest.
Public Land Order 1487 revived the Toiyabe when the Nevada National Forest was abolished effective October 1, 1957.

legacy.text: The enlarged Datil was split in December 1931, with land going to the Cibola and the Gila national forests.

today.name: Datil National Forest
today.note: Divided between the Cibola and the Gila in December 1931.

related.note: Folded the Magdalena into the Datil National Forest, which Proclamation 812 had set apart in June 1908.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 5752 transferred part of the Datil National Forest to the Cibola.
Executive Order 5765 transferred part of the Datil National Forest to the Gila.

political_impact.text: Taft's orders of February 17, 1912 removed the White Mountain Apache Reservation land this proclamation had added, restoring the reservation to its earlier status. The addition lasted barely three years.
political_impact.source: Executive Orders Relating to Indian Reservations (1912), pp. 11–12

related.note: The same day's Apache enlargement also took White Mountain Apache Reservation land and was reversed by the same 1912 orders.

later_actions.text: Taft's order excluded from the Sitgreaves all the White Mountain Apache Reservation land added by the proclamation of March 2, 1909.
later_actions.source: Executive Orders Relating to Indian Reservations (1912), pp. 11–12

related.note: Signed the same day; part of the Shasta's addition came from the Lassen, and Proclamation 867 passed two small Lassen parcels to the Shasta.

political_impact.text: The addition of Mescalero Apache Reservation land passed without recorded protest at the national level; the objections of the people affected carried little weight in the policy of the day.

legacy.text: The Alamo National Forest did not survive under that name. It was moved into the Lincoln National Forest in 1917, and the Mescalero Apache Tribe's reservation and forest lands remain a live matter of tribal sovereignty.

today.name: Lincoln National Forest
today.note: Manages the Sacramento and Guadalupe country of south-central New Mexico.

related.note: Enlarged the Alamo National Forest that Executive Order 908 formed by consolidating the Guadalupe and Sacramento forests.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2633 transferred the Alamo National Forest to the Lincoln, effective July 1, 1917.

uncertain: The full twenty-five-year Indian-rights proviso is abridged in the available text and should be reproduced verbatim from the Statutes at Large before it is quoted in full.
How much land the enlargement added is not settled: the Forest Service history's resulting total implies about 371,244 acres, while a Washington dispatch of March 7, 1909 printed 348,211.
A Washington dispatch of March 7, 1909 gave the Carson addition as 399,000 acres; the Forest Service regional history gives 444,200.

legacy.text: The Zuni was transferred whole to the Manzano National Forest in 1914, and the Manzano was renamed the Cibola in 1931.

today.name: Zuni National Forest
today.note: Transferred whole to the Manzano in 1914.

today.name: Cibola National Forest
today.note: The Manzano was renamed the Cibola in 1931.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 2045 transferred the entire Zuni National Forest to the Manzano.
Executive Order 5752 renamed the Manzano National Forest the Cibola.

political_impact.text: Part of the 1909 addition went to the Crook National Forest in 1910.
Taft's orders of February 17, 1912 returned about 348,600 acres of the Apache to the White Mountain Apache Reservation, undoing the rest of the 1909 addition.
political_impact.source: Executive Orders Relating to Indian Reservations (1912), pp. 11–12; Stark, Names, Boundaries, and Maps

related.note: The same day's Sitgreaves enlargement also took White Mountain Apache Reservation land and was reversed by the same 1912 orders.

later_actions.text: Proclamation 1088 adjusted the Apache, leaving it at 1,625,000 acres.
Taft's order excluded from the Apache all the White Mountain Apache Reservation land added by the proclamation of March 2, 1909, to restore the reservation to its earlier status.
later_actions.source: Executive Orders Relating to Indian Reservations (1912), pp. 11–12

uncertain: The addition's size, about 483,000 acres, comes from a contemporary Washington dispatch and looks like a rounded estimate for unsurveyed reservation land.

related.note: Two small Lassen parcels on the Pit River passed to the Shasta, enlarged the same day.

uncertain: A Washington dispatch of March 7, 1909 gave the Lassen addition as 517,794 acres; the Forest Service regional history gives 163,745.

reception.text: As a group the proclamations drew little notice; boundary proclamations did not make news the way the 1907 "midnight forests" had.
A Washington dispatch listed the March 2 additions forest by forest, totaling 4,980,736 acres.
reception.source: New York Lumber Trade Journal, Apr. 1, 1909, vol. 46, p. 36

reception.text: Exact-phrase searches for the three Lake States forests across 1909 in Chronicling America return eight hits, the earliest in May.

political_impact.text: Signed in the last weeks of the term, the proclamations read, where they registered at all, as the tidying-up of a departing administration.
Because the Fulton Amendment of 1907 barred new forests and additions in six Western states, not one of the thirty-six added land in Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Colorado or Wyoming.

legacy.text: Most of these forests endure with redrawn boundaries, in today's Humboldt-Toiyabe, Tonto, Gila, Tongass, Chugach, Klamath, Modoc, Sequoia, Tahoe and other national forests.
The three Lake States forests carried the national forests into Michigan and Minnesota; the Superior endures, while both Michigan forests were later absorbed into the Hiawatha.
